views/problem: Labels cost people's time: someone has to write down what each photo shows. Can a network learn to describe photos from the photos alone?
views/views: Here is a way. Cut two random crops from one photo: two views. They look different, yet they show the same thing.
views/embed: An encoder, an ordinary network, turns each view into a vector: z one for the first, and z two for the second.
views/goal: Train it so that two views of one photo point the same way, and views of different photos point apart. Each view is contrasted with the others, hence the name: contrastive.
views/simclr: In 2020, Ting Chen, Geoffrey Hinton and colleagues showed how well this works, with a recipe they called sim C L R: two random crops of every photo, recolored.
circle/arrow: Say z one comes out as six, eight. Draw it as an arrow from the origin.
circle/size: Its size as an arrow, not its count of entries, is the square root of its squared entries added up: thirty six plus sixty four is a hundred, whose square root is ten.
circle/unit: Divide each entry by ten: zero point six, zero point eight, an arrow of length one, called a unit vector. Every view is scaled this way, so every tip lands on one circle, and only directions count.
circle/sim: The similarity of two views is the dot product of their unit vectors. Pointing the same way, it is one. At a right angle, zero. Opposite, minus one.
circle/pair: Our two views sit close together, at a similarity of zero point eight.
batch/batch: Training works on a batch: a few photos at a time, each cropped twice. Here, three photos give six views.
batch/anchor: Pick one view, and call it the anchor: the one everything is measured against.
batch/pos: Its positive is the other crop of the same photo, fixed by the cropping, before anything is measured.
batch/neg: Every view of every other photo is a negative: here, four of them. Even another photo of a boat would be one: nothing says what any photo shows.
batch/grid: To keep the picture small, score each photo's first view against every second view: the positives sit on the diagonal.
batch/row: Row zero, on the circle: its anchor points straight up, the positive sits close, at zero point eight, and two negatives at zero and zero point four.
loss/ask: Now ask the anchor: of these candidates, which is your partner? It is a classification, with the positive as the right answer.
loss/range: But similarities stay between minus one and one. That is too narrow for a softmax: on this row, it gives the positive less than half.
loss/tau: So divide every similarity by a small number, the temperature, written tau, a Greek letter: here, zero point four.
loss/s: Divide by zero point four, and zero point eight becomes two, while zero point four becomes one. Zero stays zero: the gaps have stretched.
loss/heat: The name comes from physics, where this same softmax gives the odds of each state at a temperature. Hot, the odds even out; cold, one state takes nearly all.
loss/soft: Then it is the cross-entropy of a softmax, as before. e to the scores gives seven point three nine, one, and two point seven two.
loss/loss: The loss is the log of their total, eleven point one one, minus the positive's score, two: about zero point four one.
loss/oord: Aaron van den Oord and colleagues named this loss info N C E in 2018, and read it the same way: a cross-entropy for picking out the positive.
